readerTitle: The startup your CEO calls disruptive: three questions to check
caseNote: 가상 사례 (사무용품 유통사 전략팀, 동네 식료품점 체인, POS 회사 제품팀) · 판단 기준은 Christensen의 파괴적 혁신 이론
insight: '파괴적인가'는 기술이나 성장 속도로 판단하지 않는다. 누구를 먼저 공략하고, 처음에 무엇이 부족하며, 위로 올라올 길이 있는지로 판단한다.
misconception: 새롭고, 싸고, 빠르게 크는 스타트업은 모두 파괴적이다. 우리 제품보다 못한 경쟁자는 위협이 아니다.

sources.text: Christensen, C. M. (1997). The Innovator's Dilemma. Harvard Business School Press.
Christensen, C. M., Raynor, M. E., & McDonald, R. (2015). What Is Disruptive Innovation? Harvard Business Review.
모든 사업 상황은 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 모든 사업 상황(사무용품 유통사, 식료품점, POS 회사)은 가상 사례이며 실제 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다. 특정 기업을 연상시키는 이름이나 로고가 이미지에 들어가지 않는지 확인하세요.
5번 카드의 '기존 기업은 존속적 경쟁에서 대체로 이기고, 신규 진입자는 아래나 바깥에서 시작할 때 이긴다'는 Christensen(1997)과 HBR(2015)의 주장을 일반적으로 요약한 것입니다. 단정적인 통계처럼 읽히지 않는지 검토하세요.
7번 카드의 '파괴적이라는 말은 결과가 아니라 경로를 설명한다'는 HBR(2015) 글의 요지와 맞는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: "Is this startup disruptive? Answer by Friday."
body: Monday, 8:40 a.m. The CEO forwards an article to the strategy team. A young company is "set to disrupt" your industry. Her note has one line: is it?
By now the word gets used for anything new, cheap or fast-growing. Your team needs a real test, not a gut feeling. This lesson gives you three questions from earlier lessons to use as that test.

image.label: A forwarded email with the word 'disruptive?' circled
image.brief: 사무실 책상 위 노트북 화면에 전달된 이메일. 제목 줄에 "disruptive?"가 빨간 원으로 표시됨. 옆에 식은 커피잔과 포스트잇 세 장("Who?", "Worse at?", "Path up?"). 실제 회사 로고나 메일 서비스 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A cheaper, thinner rival appears.
body: You're on the strategy team of a large office-supplies distributor. You serve big companies with a huge range, next-day delivery and account managers.
A startup sells a much smaller range online to small shops and freelancers. No account manager, slower delivery, lower prices. What do you tell the CEO?

options.text: Not disruptive. Its offer is worse than ours on every point our clients care about
options.feedback: Being worse for your best customers is exactly how disruption starts. A rival that beat you on your own terms would be a *sustaining* competitor, and incumbents usually win those races.

options.text: Yes, disruptive. It's cheaper and it's online
options.feedback: Cheap and online are clues, not proof. What matters is who it serves first and whether it can improve toward your core accounts.

options.text: Possibly. It serves customers we overserve with a simpler, cheaper offer. We should watch whether it moves up
options.feedback: That's the **low-end disruption** test: good enough for customers who pay for more than they need, with room to improve. You get a real answer and a thing to monitor.

cards.title: Three questions before you use the word.
body: Run any new rival through these, in order:
list: **Better on what our best customers value?** Then it's sustaining. You can usually match it.
**Good enough and cheaper for customers who get more than they need?** That's a low-end foothold.
**Reaching people who buy nothing today?** That's a new-market foothold.
**Can it keep improving toward our core customers?** Without this, it stays a niche.
cards.callout: Disruptive means the rival starts below or outside your best customers, then climbs.
cards.softwareNote: The same test works for software. A simple tool for teams too small for your product, at a fraction of the price, is a low-end or new-market foothold, even if your feature list is far longer.

cards.title: The distributor's startup, scored.
body: Put together, this looks like a **low-end foothold**. The real question for the CEO is the last row: how fast is its range growing, and are any mid-sized firms switching yet?

breakdown.label: Who it serves first
breakdown.detail: Customers you treat as minor accounts

breakdown.label: Where it's worse
breakdown.detail: Matters most to your big clients

breakdown.label: Path up
breakdown.detail: The signal to watch each quarter

cards.title: Dismissing a weaker rival is the classic mistake.
body: Clayton Christensen's research made a simple point. When a newcomer tries to beat leaders at their own game, leaders usually respond and win. They have the customers, the money and the motive.

When a newcomer starts with a cheaper or simpler offer for customers the leader doesn't value, the leader has little reason to fight. Those customers look small and unprofitable. So the newcomer grows quietly, improves, and only later reaches the leader's best customers.

cards.title: Two new grocers open near your stores.
body: You own three mid-sized grocery stores with a wide range and a deli counter.

One newcomer is an upscale market with better produce and higher prices. The other is a small discount store with far fewer products, mostly its own brands, and low prices. Which one fits the disruption pattern?

options.text: The upscale market. It's better than you on quality
options.feedback: It competes for your best customers on terms they already care about. That's **sustaining** competition. It can hurt, but you can answer with better produce of your own.

options.text: The discount store. It's worse on choice but good enough for many shoppers
options.feedback: That's **low-end disruption**: it wins shoppers who pay for range they don't use. If it keeps adding products, it climbs toward your core.

options.text: Neither. They're both just new competitors
options.feedback: True, but the label changes your response. The upscale rival needs a direct reply. The discount one needs watching before it looks like a threat.

cards.title: Disruptive doesn't mean dangerous, or doomed.
body: The label describes a *path*, not an outcome. Many low-end entrants stay at the bottom because they never improve. Some sustaining rivals do far more damage in the short run.
Use the test in both directions. Don't wave off a weak rival just because it's weak. And don't panic about every cheap newcomer. The useful output is a short list of signals to watch, not a verdict.

cards.title: Your product team sees a tiny rival.
body: You lead product at a company selling checkout systems to restaurants and shops.
A startup offers a phone app that lets street-food stalls and market sellers take cards and track sales. Most of these sellers use a cash box today. Which idea best describes this rival?

options.text: Sustaining. It's a payments product, just like ours
options.feedback: Same category, different game. It isn't trying to be better for your restaurant clients, so matching its features misses the point.

options.text: Low-end disruption. It's cheaper and simpler than our system
options.feedback: Cheaper and simpler, yes. But these sellers weren't buying from you at all, so it isn't pulling away your overserved customers.

options.text: New-market disruption. It serves people who buy nothing like this today
options.feedback: That's **new-market disruption**: it competes with the cash box, not with you. Watch for small cafés starting to use it.

cards.title: Ask who, worse at what, and what's the path up.
body: You used three ideas from this unit: **sustaining vs disruptive change** to rule out rivals who fight on your terms, **low-end disruption** for good-enough offers to overserved customers, and **new-market disruption** for rivals who serve people buying nothing today.
**Try it today:** pick one newcomer in your market. Write who it serves first, where it's worse than you, and one sign that it's moving up.
